cards.back: About 2,000 non-technical users over about 800 BigQuery tables; answers within 30 s at p95. Start with the 50 to 100 curated tables most questions use.

cards.front: What goes in the schema index
cards.back: One card per table: description, columns with types and PII tags, join keys and grain, example questions, freshness and owner. Metadata, never rows.
Fixed definitions of metrics like revenue and signups (dbt metrics, LookML, Cube), so two people asking the same thing get the same number.

cards.front: Run every query as the user
cards.back: OAuth on behalf of the signed-in user, so BigQuery enforces their own access and the audit log names them. A shared service account is the most common security mistake.
Column profiles computed in code: type, null rate, distinct count, and value lists only for safe low-cardinality columns.
Single SELECT only, no unaggregated PII columns, a dry-run bytes cap, and a row limit and timeout enforced by the runner.
Run the agent's SQL and the analyst's SQL and compare results, ignoring order and rounding. Target 90% or more offline; never grade the SQL text with an LLM judge.
About 500 past analyst tickets with question, SQL and answer, stratified by team and question type, plus questions that should be declined.
Live proxies (thumbs, rephrase within 2 minutes, SQL error and empty rate, decline rate), a weekly graded sample of 50 answers, and zero-tolerance safety alerts.
Any access violation is an instant kill. Thumbs-down above 15% for 3 days or graded accuracy below 85% pulls back to the pilot group.
Schema retrieval under 1 s, SQL generation 3 to 8 s, BigQuery 2 to 15 s, chart and explanation 2 to 4 s, under 30 s total at p95.

quiz.q: A sales rep got a finance number by phrasing the question cleverly. The agent runs queries with one service account. What is the fix?
choices: A stricter system prompt
Run every query as the signed-in user so BigQuery enforces their own access
Remove finance tables from the schema index
An LLM judge on each answer
quiz.why: A shared service account has the union of everyone's access; running as the user caps it at that person's rights.

quiz.q: To help the model, someone adds 5 sample rows to each table card. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing; examples improve SQL
Sample rows make cards too long for retrieval
They put customer names and emails into every prompt that retrieves the table, breaking the PII requirement
BigQuery forbids reading rows
quiz.why: Use column profiles computed in code instead of raw values.

quiz.q: Cost per question is 3× budget; BigQuery bytes, not tokens, dominate. What do you tighten first?
choices: The dry-run bytes cap and partition filters
Switch to a smaller model
Drop the chart step
Lower the row limit only
quiz.why: Bytes scanned usually costs more than the model; the dry-run cap and partition filters bound it.

quiz.q: Two queries look nothing alike but return the same numbers as the analyst's. How should the eval score them?
choices: Have an LLM judge rate SQL similarity
Fail both; they differ from the reference SQL
Score by token overlap with the analyst's SQL
Both pass on execution accuracy, since results match
quiz.why: Execution accuracy compares results, because different queries can both be right.

quiz.q: Thumbs-down has been 17% for three days, with no access violations. What does the design do?
choices: Instant kill switch for all users
Pull back to the pilot group and investigate
Nothing until the weekly sample
Raise the decline rate
quiz.why: Thumbs-down above 15% for 3 days triggers a pull back to the pilot; the kill switch is for access violations.

quiz.q: The SQL error rate on one table jumps after a dbt release renamed columns. What is the mitigation?
choices: Rebuild table cards from dbt on every deploy
Add sample rows to the card
Retry the query three times
Grade it in the weekly sample
quiz.why: Schema drift is caught by SQL error rate per table and fixed by rebuilding cards from dbt each deploy.

quiz.q: Two teams get different revenue numbers for the same question. What is the design's fix?
choices: Let the model pick the newest table
Show both numbers
One governed metric definition in the semantic layer
Ban the word revenue
quiz.why: A semantic layer gives fixed definitions so the same question gets the same number.
